cells.tense: Right now the open front is doing its work, and the person who carries the weight knows it's there.
cells.ask: Name one thing you can feel but haven't put words to — one sentence, written or spoken, saying what's underneath. Watch what shifts when it gets to be said instead of kept.
cells.core:
You can bear weight and stay open at the same time, and that combination is rarer than it looks. Feelings arrive without you deciding they should, and nothing in you rushes to label them or push them off. The strength and the openness are feeding each other while you carry.

A packed kitchen, three things on the stove and someone talking — you're following the conversation and not missing the pot about to boil over. The hearing is clean and the bearing is steady. Name one feeling you've been keeping quiet and put it in a sentence, to yourself if nowhere else — a feeling that gets named is what keeps the channel open for whatever comes next.
cells.sheetLine: You can carry weight and stay soft while you do it.
cells.verb: opening to what's here before you know what it is
cells.place: the part of a life that holds what has to be held

cells.tense: Ahead of where you actually are, you're already braced — planning loads nobody's handed you and outcomes you can't write in.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you're braced for that hasn't happened yet, and put the date next to it. Notice how much of what you carry is going into a day that may not arrive.
cells.core:
You're spending what you can bear on things that haven't happened. Anticipating what the people around you will need, shielding against outcomes that aren't here, bracing before the next blow — so the open front keeps getting jammed shut by a future you're already living in. The bracing is costing you the room to feel what's here.

A Sunday evening with the week already pressing in — you haven't done anything wrong, you're just carrying Monday and Tuesday and the thing on Thursday that may not happen at all. That's the shape of it. Say one of those out loud: 'I'm braced for ___ on ___.' Then look around the room and name one thing actually in it.
cells.sheetLine: You're braced for a blow that hasn't landed.

cells.tense: Behind where you actually are, a door you already walked through is still being stood at — and the standing is where the feeling went.
cells.ask: One morning this week, sit somewhere ordinary and name one thing you're feeling — even if it's only 'tired' or 'fine' — and say it plainly to yourself. No fixing it, no meaning it has to carry.
cells.core:
You know how to hold on, and somewhere along the way the front got sealed to hold more. The feeling that would tell you what you actually need is quiet, so you keep bearing it on your own, without the signal that would let you set it down. What's gone missing isn't strength. It's the simple reception of what's here — a feeling coming in before it gets sorted.

A kitchen bench at the end of the day, a cup in your hands, nobody asking you for anything for five minutes — that's where this belongs, not in a harder push. Name one thing you can feel in your body right now, warm or tight or tired, and let it be there. Feeling it isn't a breach of duty. It's the part of you that knows what to do next getting a signal.
cells.sheetLine: You went closed to keep carrying, and the weight didn't lighten.

cells.tense: The pen is down, and the room you're already writing in is one you keep calling borrowed — the feeling is yours and it's been filed under something else.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've felt today that you've been calling 'just tired' or 'overreacting'. Say what it actually is, in one sentence, with no frame around it. Notice what changes when it gets to be plain.
cells.core:
You're already receiving — reading the room, feeling what hasn't been said, taking in more than gets named. But the caption on it says otherwise, so the openness gets credited to someone else's mood or the day's luck. The front is open; the claim that it's yours is what's missing.

A kitchen full of people and you're the one who can feel the temperature shift before anyone speaks — that's the reception working, and it's yours. Pick one feeling you've had today that you've been framing as something else: tiredness that's really something, patience that's really grief, fine that's really none of the above. Say the plain name once, out loud or on paper. See what the day does with a feeling allowed to be what it is.
cells.sheetLine: You're already feeling it. The saying is what's left.

attempts.check: The draft keeps the person's story out of it: what's rendered is the shape of a capacity — the open front and the load it bears — not a claim about what anyone lived through. The reader could reasonably say the heart is more defended here than open, so each cell names a condition to try, not a verdict on what's true. The asks survive being wrong: each one leaves a mark a camera could see today and teaches something whether or not the read lands. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is the one reaching for a diagnosis; I've cut those and left a pattern to check, not a proof of biography.
